h1: The 5 Best Leaf Blower Vacuum Combos of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Leaf Blower Vacuum Combos: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: five leaf blower, vacuum and mulcher combos, from cord-free kits to budget electrics, with the tradeoffs of each.
summary: The WORX Trivac 3-in-1 is the best overall: an electric blower, vacuum and mulcher in the $50 to $100 bucket. The EGO Power+ LV5000 is the cordless pick, with a stated 500 CFM. BLACK+DECKER offers a mid-price battery kit rated at 120 MPH. The Heywork lists 450 CFM at the lowest bucket, and the MZK is the low-cost electric.
intro: A tool that blows, vacuums and mulches can replace two machines in the shed, but only if you will really convert it between modes. Plenty of shoppers chase the biggest number on the page and then dread swapping the tube every autumn, so the first question is how you plan to use it. If you only blow leaves into piles, a combo is a more complicated way to own a blower.

We reviewed five combos from spec sheets and listing details and ranked them on the Primea framework. Power source, airflow, versatility and price bucket carried the most weight. Several listings omit airflow, and we mark those gaps plainly rather than assume the number. That honesty matters more than a tidy table.

products.name: WORX Trivac 3-in-1 Electric Leaf Blower/Leaf Vacuum/Leaf Mulcher
products.verdict: The most complete blower, vacuum and mulcher in one electric unit.
products.description:
The WORX Trivac is the combo to buy when you want all three jobs covered on a modest budget. It is an electric 3-in-1 that blows, vacuums and mulches, in the $50 to $100 bucket. Mulching shrinks leaves so a bag holds far more, which is the main reason to own a vacuum mode at all.

It ranks first because it covers every mode at a modest price from a known brand. The EGO costs $200 to $500 for cordless freedom, and the BLACK+DECKER kit costs $100 to $200. The Heywork and MZK cost less but come with less certainty.

Buy it for a small to medium yard near an outlet. The caveat is the missing airflow: the listing gives no CFM or MPH, so you cannot compare its power with the others. A cord also limits reach on a large lot.
products.idealFor: Homeowners wanting one electric tool for leaf cleanup.
products.skipIf: You need cordless freedom across a large yard.

products.name: EGO Power+ LV5000 Leaf Vacuum and Mulcher with 500 CFM Blower
products.verdict: Battery-powered with a stated 500 CFM blower.
products.description:
The EGO Power+ LV5000 is the strongest numbers on the list. It lists 500 CFM, runs on battery, and vacuums, mulches and blows. Battery power removes the extension cord, which matters on a large lot or around trees where cords snag.

It ranks second because it is the only combo with a stated airflow figure at a high bucket, but it costs $200 to $500, much more than the WORX Trivac. Against the BLACK+DECKER kit, it lists CFM where the other lists only speed, so you can see what you are buying.

Choose it for a large yard where cord-free freedom matters and you want a measurable figure. The caveat is runtime: battery tools stop when the pack runs out, so check whether the battery and charger are included in the box.
products.idealFor: Larger yards where a cord is a nuisance.
products.skipIf: You want to spend as little as possible.

products.name: BLACK+DECKER Leaf Blower Cordless Leaf Vacuum and Mulcher Combo Kit
products.verdict: A battery-powered kit with a 120 MPH blower at a middle price.
products.description:
The BLACK+DECKER kit pairs a cordless blower with a cordless vacuum and mulcher. It lists 120 MPH, battery power and a two-tool kit format, at $100 to $200. Speed at the nozzle helps lift stuck debris such as damp leaves on a lawn.

It ranks third because the listing gives speed but no CFM, so you cannot tell how much air it moves. Compared with the EGO, you save a bracket but lose the stated airflow. Compared with the WORX, you gain battery freedom but pay more. The kit format means two separate tools rather than one convertible machine.

Choose it if you want to blow and vacuum without a cord and prefer separate tools. The caveat is that separate tools take more storage space.
products.idealFor: Cordless buyers who stop short of the top price bucket.
products.skipIf: You want a stated CFM rating.

products.name: Heywork 3-in-1 Leaf Vacuum Mulcher
products.description:
The Heywork 3-in-1 is the budget route to a stated airflow figure. It lists 450 CFM and three modes in the $25 to $50 bucket. A stated CFM is useful because it lets you compare it with the EGO at 500 CFM directly.

It ranks fourth because the power source is not listed. That is a real gap: you do not know whether it needs a cord or a battery, which changes how you use it. Cheap tools also leave more questions about build quality and parts support, and the listing offers few details.

Buy it if you want to try a combo at the lowest price and are happy to verify the power type before ordering. The caveat is that missing information. Ask the seller before buying, and compare it against the WORX Trivac, which at least states electric.
products.idealFor: Budget buyers wanting a stated airflow figure.
products.skipIf: You want a well-documented spec sheet.

products.name: MZK 3-in-1 Electric Leaf Blower Vacuum Mulcher
products.verdict: An electric 3-in-1 in the lowest price bucket.
products.description:
The MZK is a low-cost electric 3-in-1 that blows, vacuums and mulches. It costs $25 to $50 and gives no airflow figure in the listing. A cord means unlimited runtime but a tether to the nearest outlet.

It ranks last because it offers the fewest stated numbers. The Heywork lists 450 CFM at the same bucket, and the WORX Trivac states electric power for a bit more. Without airflow, you cannot judge how it will handle wet leaves or a large pile.

Buy it for a small patio, a driveway or a yard with a nearby outlet. The caveat is that missing performance data: treat a missing number as a reason to ask questions, not as a good sign, and plan to keep it light duty.
products.idealFor: Occasional users with a small yard.

whatMatters.detail: CFM measures how much air is moved, while MPH measures air speed at the nozzle. Volume matters for pushing wet or heavy piles and speed matters for lifting stuck debris. The EGO lists 500 CFM, the Heywork 450 CFM and the BLACK+DECKER 120 MPH. Look for both numbers in the bullets, and distrust a listing that gives neither.

A corded electric combo runs as long as you have an outlet, while a battery tool gives freedom but limited runtime. The choice matters on larger yards where an extension cord gets in the way. Check whether the battery and charger are included in the box, because they are the costliest parts of a cordless combo. A bare tool price can hide a second purchase.

A mulcher shreds leaves so they take up less space in a bag, which matters if you collect leaves instead of blowing them away. Confirm that the listing says mulcher, not just vacuum, as on the WORX Trivac and EGO LV5000, and check whether a mulch ratio is listed.

Combos need you to swap tubes or attachments between jobs. If that is awkward you will skip using the vacuum and the machine becomes an expensive blower. Read the listing for how the conversion works, and look at photos of the attachments. A kit with separate tools, like the BLACK+DECKER, avoids conversion altogether, at the cost of storing two tools instead of one.

A lower bucket often means fewer documented specs, which matters because you cannot compare what is not stated. The MZK and WORX Trivac list no airflow figure, and the Heywork does not list its power source. Treat missing numbers as a reason to ask questions, not as a good sign.

faq.q: Can one tool really blow, vacuum and mulch?
faq.a: Yes, the combos here advertise all three. You usually swap an attachment between jobs, so check how the conversion works before buying a WORX Trivac or similar, because an awkward swap means the vacuum mode goes unused.

faq.q: What is the common mistake with these?
faq.a: Buying on the biggest number without checking the power source. A cord can limit a large yard, while a battery adds runtime limits. Check whether the Heywork lists either one, since its listing names neither, and confirm the plug or pack before you order.

faq.q: Is the EGO worth it over the WORX?
faq.a: Only if you want cordless and a stated 500 CFM. Otherwise the WORX Trivac is a lower bucket for the same three jobs, and it runs without a battery to charge.

faq.q: How do I set one up?
faq.a: Attach the tube for your chosen mode and follow the listing's conversion steps. Read the manual before first use, and fit the collection bag securely before you switch the vacuum on, since a loose bag spills debris back across the lawn.

faq.q: How do I maintain a mulcher?
faq.a: Clear the intake and the bag after use. Keep the inlet free of wet clumps, and do not mulch damp, matted leaves in the EGO or WORX, because wet clumps jam the impeller and stall the motor.

faq.q: Does a listing that lacks CFM mean it is weak?
faq.a: Not necessarily, but you cannot verify it. The WORX Trivac and MZK both omit airflow, so treat the missing number as a gap, look for owner comments on suction, and ask the seller for the CFM before you commit.

finalTake: Buy the WORX Trivac for a simple electric combo at a modest price. Step up to the EGO LV5000 if you want a battery and a stated airflow figure. The BLACK+DECKER kit sits in between, and the Heywork and MZK are the budget options. Whatever you pick, confirm that the mulching function is real and that the power source suits your yard.
